## 1 Rationale and Research Questions

The purpose of this study is to analyze the spatial distribution of invasive species across three study sites on the Big Island of Hawai‘i. Prior to Polynesian arrival in the remote Pacific, new invasive species established naturally at an estimated rate of one species every 50,000 years. After Polynesian settlement, this rate increased to roughly three to four species every hundred years (Young 2016). Following European contact, the introduction rate accelerated dramatically to approximately twenty invasive species per year in Hawai‘i (Ewell 1999). While non-native species include any organisms introduced outside their natural range, only a subset of them become invasive. Invasive species are defined as non-native organisms that spread rapidly and/or cause ecological, economic, or cultural harm. These invasive species pose a substantial threat to Hawai‘i’s unique native biota. Of the roughly 10,000 native species found across the Hawaiian Islands, nearly 90% are endemic—occurring nowhere else on Earth. Our goal is to evaluate the invasive species on the Big Island across three study sites over the past thirteen years to inform best management practices to protect endemic species of the Hawaiian Islands. Our dataset focuses on three sites on the Big Island: Mauna Loa, Ola’a, and Nahuku/East Rift. Mauna Loa is classified as a subalpine shrubland, and Ola’a and Nahuku/East Rift are considered wet forest habitats. Our dataset ranges from 2010 to 2023 and contains coordinates for each survey site where a transect was used to count species-level observations and counts of repeated occurrences. **Through our analysis, we aim to answer the following research questions:

1.  Does invasive species' richness change across the three sample regions?
2.  Does invasive species' structural diversity change across the three sample regions?
3.  How does the frequency and distribution of invasive species change over time for each site?**

We hypothesize that there will be a significant difference in species richness and structural diversity between habitats and vegetation types. Previous research in Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park shows that there is a sharp transition between wet forests and subalpine habitats. A Hawaiian treeline ecotones study attributed the phenomenon to distinct changes in altitude, soil moisture, and wind patterns (Ainsworth and Drake 2024). We predict that both wet forest types will have a more rapid increase in invasive species introduction over time than Mauna Loa. This expectation is based on reduced physical barriers (e.g., less steep terrain, increased connectivity with other habitat types), higher resource availability, more human/animal activity to disperse propagules, and a wider range of ecological niches for invasive species to occupy.

## 2 Dataset Information

Raw data was derived from the United States Government's open data site starting from October 4th, 2010 to September 7th, 2023. This dataset is part of The Pacific Island Inventory and Monitoring Network (PACN) Established Invasive Plant Species (EIPS) Monitoring Protocol. More information on the sources used can be found in the table below:

```{r dataset.information, fig.cap = "Table 2.1: Dataset Information on PACN EIPS Cover Class Data", echo = FALSE}

#Create a dataframe with dataset information
Dataset.Information <- data.frame (
  Detail = c("Name", "Publisher", "Retrieved From", "Variables Used", "Date Range"),
  Description = c("Pacific Island Network Established Invasive Plant Species Monitoring Dataset 2010-2022", "National Park Service", "https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/pacific-island-network-established-invasive-plant-species-monitoring-dataset-2010-2022", "Plant Community, Sampling Frame, Decimal Latitude, Decimal Longitude, Date, Species Code, Scientific Name, Vernacular Name, Vegetation Type", "October 4, 2010 to September 7, 2023")
)

knitr::kable(Dataset.Information,
             col.names = c("Detail", "Description"),
             digits = 2)
```

## 3 Exploratory Analysis

### 3.1 Exploration of Raw Data

The raw dataset included 37977 observations across 33 variables, including sampling date, plant community (e.g., wet forest, subalpine shrubland), transect number and type, transect latitude and longitude, datum, species, and life form (which we later refer to as “vegetation type”), among others.

```{r RawData, echo=FALSE}
CoverClass_Data <- 
  read.csv("Data/Raw/PACN_EIPS_Cover_Class_Data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

str(CoverClass_Data)
```

### 3.2 Study Site

Three regions within Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park were selected as the Big Island contained the most sampling sites out of all the Hawaiian Islands in the dataset. All invasive plant species were counted within 5 × 20 m plots at each site, allowing for comparison between wet forest and subalpine shrubland habitats. *Figure 1* displays a Landsat mosaic of the approximate location and average elevation of our three study regions. In *Figure 2*, sampling sites are color-coded by region. Mauna Loa, the subalpine shrubland, is depicted in orange. Wet forest habitat types are shown in blue, with Nāhuku/East Rift in light blue and Ola‘a in dark blue.

```{r Image, fig.cap="Figure 3.2: Landsat Mosaic of Big Island of Hawaii, Average Elevation (m)", out.width = "50%", echo = FALSE, messages = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("Data/Processed/BigIsland.png")

```

```{r Map of Sampling Sites, fig.cap = "Map showing the sampling sites are color-coded by region", echo = FALSE}

BigIsland_Processed <- 
  read.csv("Data/Processed/BigIsland_Processed.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  
hawaii.counties <- st_read("Data/Raw/cb_2018_us_county_20m.shp")%>%
filter(STATEFP == 15 )

big_island <- hawaii.counties %>% 
  filter(NAME == "Hawaii")

sites_sf <- st_as_sf(BigIsland_Processed, coords = c("Decimal_Longitude","Decimal_Latitude"), crs = 4326) 

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=big_island, fill="lightgreen",
          color="forestgreen") +
  geom_sf(data = sites_sf, 
          aes(color = BigIsland_Processed$Sampling_Frame), 
          size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
  values = c(
    "Mauna Loa" = "orange2",
    "Nahuku / East Rift" = "lightblue",
    "Olaa" = "steelblue" ))+
  hawaiitheme+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))+
  labs(title = "Sampling Locations on the Big Island",
       color = "Sampling Sites")
```

### 3.3 Data Wrangling

After preliminary raw data exploration, we filtered for the three sampling sites (Mauna Loa, Nahuku/East Rift, and Ola’a) on the Big Island of Hawai’i. We selected the following variables that better suit our analyses and renamed each column by removing “custom\_” prefix: Plant Community, Sampling Frame, Decimal Latitude, Decimal Longitude, Date, Species Code, Scientific Name, Vernacular Name, and Vegetation Type. The wrangled, processed dataset was saved as “BigIsland_Processed.csv”. Another dataset, “BigIsland_Clean.csv”, was used to conduct ANOVA and Tukey Post-Hoc tests as these statistical analyses required transect numbers.

## 4 Analysis

```{r Research Question 1, fig.cap="Figure 4.1: Overall Invasive Species Richness at Each Site\non the Big Island of Hawai'i", echo = FALSE}

#Note: In the title names I added "\n" to create new line breaks to prevent text from disappearing from the screen, so they are NOT typos!
Invasive_Richness <- ggplot(BigIsland_Processed, aes(x = Sampling_Frame, fill = Sampling_Frame)) +
 geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Overall Invasive Species Richness at Each Site\non the Big Island of Hawai'i",
    subtitle = "Wet Forest in Blue | Subalpine Shrubland in Orange",
    x = "Sample Region",
    y = "Species Count"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Mauna Loa" = "orange2",
                    "Olaa" = "steelblue",
                    "Nahuku / East Rift" = "lightblue"),
                    guide = "none")
  
print(Invasive_Richness)
```

**Site Region Richness:** Our results support our hypothesis that Mauna Loa had the lowest overall invasive species richness compared to other regions (Figure 4.1). Higher elevation environments such as Mauna Loa tend to experience less invasive species; likely due to harsher environmental conditions, short growing seasons, and steep terrain that limit their persistence. Notably, Ola’a has the lowest average elevation and the greatest invasive species richness (Figure 4.1). Lower elevations tend to have milder climates that support favorable conditions for diverse species growth and proliferation (Ainsworth and Drake 2024).

Our ANOVA test revealed that there was a significant difference in overall invasive species richness between Ola’a and Mauna Loa (p-value of 0.028). There was no meaningful significance in invasive species richness between Nahuku / East Rift and Mauna Loa (p-value of 0.161) and Ola’a and Nahuku / East Rift (p-value of 0.803). We chose to define richness as the number of distinct species types at a given transect by using the function “n_distinct”, negating repeated counts of species occurrence. In doing so, we were able to assign richness scores to each transect and averaged across study regions to determine their respective invasive species richness. After running a Tukey Post-Hoc Test, we found that Ola’a has an overall higher invasive species richness relative to Mauna Loa.

```{r Research Question 2, fig.cap="Invasive Species Richness by Vegetation Type\nat Each Site on the Big Island of Hawai'i", echo=FALSE}
Invasive_Richness_Type1 <- ggplot(BigIsland_Processed, aes(x = Vegetation_Type, fill = Sampling_Frame)) +
 geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    title = "Invasive Species Richness by Vegetation Type\nat Each Site on the Big Island of Hawai'i",
    subtitle = "Wet Forest in Blue | Subalpine Shrubland in Orange",
    x = "Vegetation Type",
    y = "Species Count"
    ) +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("Mauna Loa" = "orange2",
                    "Olaa" = "steelblue",
                    "Nahuku / East Rift" = "lightblue"))
  
print(Invasive_Richness_Type1)
```
Regional Structural Diversity: An ANOVA test analyzing the significance of structural differences between study regions found that Nahuku / East Rift, Ola’a, and Mauna Loa all had significant differences in structural diversity. By aggregating the number of vegetation types found at each transect/sampling point, we are able to determine the structural diversity of a given point and translate regional patterns into comparable data that is then analyzed for statistical significance (i.e. a site with tree + shrub + fern + grass receives a diversity score of 4, whereas a site with only grass + shrub receives diversity score of 2). A Tukey Post-Hoc test revealed that Ola’a has a greater structural diversity than Mauna Loa with a mean difference of 4.527. Nahuku-East Rift is also more structurally diverse than Mauna Loa with a mean difference of 3.081. Ola’a also has a higher structural diversity than Nahuku / East Rift with a mean difference of 1.446, though this difference is comparably less pronounced. This suggests that overall, Ola’a has the greatest structural diversity, followed by Nahuku / East Rift, and Mauna Loa with the lowest structural diversity.
